content: This is the discussion thread for #Project announcements > Hex: graph isomorphism via a formalization of `nauty`

My apologies, @Alex Meiburg, I hadn't seen the discussion around your #Project announcements > IsoGraph: Graph library until I came to Zulip to post the announcement for this.

(I only started implementation last Tuesday.)
Not my area at all but this sounds really cool.

Ah nice! :) Yes, definitely plenty of overlap here with IsoGraph; it would be great if we could combine it somehow!

IsoGraph also has a verified "small nauty-like" automorphism algorithm, in order to show isomorphism or not; so in that sense the goals are very aligned. Quite possible that your implementation is faster (I didn't go _super_ hard on performance) in which case it might be a nice drop-in replacement. My implementation does offer generators as part of the API, so that you can easily certify [non-]vertex transitivity, edge-transitivity, or arc-transitivity as well.

There are other algorithms implemented that, I'm guessing, you might find useful as well, like subgraph testing/minor testing, decomposition, or calculating invariants like independence and chromatic numbers. If that would be welcome in a future putative "HexGraph", maybe it would make sense to progressively merge them in some form?

IsoGraph is, at the moment, quite interlinked with Mathlib; but I also don't think it would be terrible to separate this in the Hex-style "with" and "without" Mathlib halves.

@Alex Meiburg, did you compare your algorithm against nauty? HexGraphIso appears to just be a constant (~10) factor slower. nauty has received decades of attention from the experts; I suspect it just doesn't make sense to implement anything except faithful translations.

In the meantime I've added the unverified functions for enumerating generators, and I think the verification looks easy once some quotas reset. :-)

But yes, if you have good algorithms for the things you list, I would love to add them to HexGraph*. To be honest I think the best approach is to write clear SPEC/Libraries/HexGraphX.md files, saying which algorithms we want, what the interface should be, and our performance expectations, and then just say "/goal Please implement X.md as a Hex library, after carefully reviewing the previous implementation at Z.", rather than actually trying to merge code.
@Alex Meiburg, woah, on initial profiling IsoGraph looks really good. Digging a bit, but I'll post some graphs soon.
Excited to hear the report!

Sorry, still coming. the basic answer is that IsoGraph is much faster on sparse graphs, than either HexGraphIso or (eventually) even dense nauty, but on dense graphs it is slower. IsoGraph however is still slower (unsuprising) than Traces / sparse nauty (which hasn't been translated to Lean, but now thinking about it :-)

I want to squeeze a bit more performance out of HexGraphIso too, but the AIs got bogged down in a big cleanup I tried to do first.
Ah, makes sense! Interesting.

Here's the five way comparison (HexGraphIso, IsoGraph, nauty dense, nauty sparse, Traces), on a benchmark set of families.

IsoGraph basically beats HexGraphIso everywhere, except the projective plane and shrunken millipede families. So I have work to do. :-) But that work is mainly to realize I translated/formalized the wrong target, i.e. dense nauty rather than sparse nauty (or possibly Traces, which is very fast on some families, and blows up on others).

Astra is making plans now. :-)
Great, good luck to you and Astra! :) And good forensics!

I have to say, I am really enjoying this project. Being able to take software like nauty and tell an AI "please translate this to Lean and prove that it is correct", and have it basically come out right, is just a lovely superpower. As soon as we have sparse nauty translated, let's try to work out a plan to integrate / cross-link / etc these implementations.

Here's the first cut of the translation of sparse nauty. (No proofs yet, just a Lean re-implementation.)

That already looks promising. Still significantly slower that IsoGraph for smaller graphs, but later overtakes.

(This is a cactus plot combining all the families from the chart above. It's not particularly scientific!)

Okay, I've finished the formalization of the translation of sparse nauty.

The performance looks really good.
Great :)
Now, about all the lovely additional functionality that IsoGraph has... :-)

Yes; I'm pretty happy with how I set up a lot of the library (as e.g. a library for working with small graphs), how open would you be to 'just' porting it over? (Porting it to use your definition of graph, that is, but most algorithms/proofs/definitions otherwise go unchanged; a toIsoGraph attribute mostly identical to the current one.)

Or -- what is your vision for what 'belongs' in HexGraphIso?
Sorry, which direction? Porting stuff from GraphIso to HexGraphIso, or the other direction? I'm pretty happy to do either.

Sorry, I mean: IsoGraph also has stuff like a lot of definitions of graph invariants, a library of small graphs, and a bunch of theorems about those invariants on particular [families of] graphs. I don't know if you feel like those belong in HexGraphIso.

I understand that porting stuff like minor testing to HexGraphIso would be an obvious next step. But if you feel like the small graphs and invariants belong as well, then I could look at just trying to port all of IsoGraph over in one effort. (Not necessarily one PR, but one push of work to port it all, that can then be merged in a few passes.)

Of course I'd also be happy to port your faster isomorphism testing algorithm to IsoGraph. :) But I'm also realizing that, realistically, IsoGraph won't likely get many "users" as it stands; something that's part of Hex stands a better chance of actually being useful to someone some day!
